title: Puffed cheeks and jaw: Brunies and other trombonists
summary: Cheek-puffing in Louis Armstrong and George Brunies, and how Palmer changed his own style.

story.theme_name: The reed and horn player's craft: clarinet, sax, tone
story.community_name: Cornet or trumpet: choosing and owning horns

blocks.x: Here's another question. I keep changing the subject, but I think about it. Louis' neck puffs out so when he plays.
Did you ever have any trouble like that? No, I never did do that. And puffing the jaw.
Is there anything you can tell people?

I brought it from the throat, just right from the throat, right out of the throat. I never puffed my jaw. I don't know why they do that. Very seldom, very seldom I'd puff my jaw. Not on pedal, even on pedal notes, I wouldn't puff my jaw.
There's one trombonist there, George Brunus, a white fellow from New Orleans.

Oh, no, that boy, I know him. He just come from over in our jays. He come from across the river. We come up together on here. George Brunus and Milton Brunus, his brother. Yeah. And I forget this other boy. There was another boy come up here with an orchestra.
Paul Merez. Yeah, Paul Merez. Well, there was another trombonist down there, Tom Brown. Yeah, Tom Brown. Oh, he had a band.
He came up there pretty early. I remember him. I remember him.
Anyway, Brunus puffs out just one cheek. Just one cheek, yeah. Is he playing here? Yeah, he's up at the 11-11 Club at Bryn Mawr. Yeah? On the north side. He's been here for four years.

Another boy, too, was with them. I forget his name. He played trumpet. He quit playing, though. He's from downtown. What is that fellow's name? I couldn't think of a name. Jelliro knew them all. But Brunus is a raised trombone player, a puff boy. He's in jail like that.
Is there anything you can do about that?

Yeah, he's just laying off a trombone. He'd have to lay off trombone about two or three months and change the style of playing. I had a style of playing, too. And I changed that style. I saw it wasn't no good and it prevented me from making quick passages. You know, see? All that stops you. You see that wind. You got drawed back in there. And you're trying to execute with the instrument. It's very hard. A good trombone player, but they're lazy and slow. You know, they ain't got that snap, see? They can't do it, see? Because the jaw is full of wind. And they're trying to make quick passages. And that wind got to come way back up here.
